brief_bullets: Kolkata Police issue 11-point advisory; CM Adhikari hints at scrapping VIP entries at major pandals Among the 19 dead are 13 females, including two minors; the two other deceased minors are males Kolkata’s Bonedi Bari Durga pujas bring together grand colonial-era architecture, family legacies and heirloom recipes.

While the city’s pandals draw the biggest crowds, these ancestral homes offer a more intimate glimpse of the festival, following family traditions dating back more than 300 years Durga Puja celebrations mean glitzy pandals, excessive lighting, high-decibel music and many more attractions.But several committees organising the annual Durga Puja in Kokrajhar town in western Assam, the district headquarters of the Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR), have pitched in to adopt the concept of “carbon-neutral” celebrations by planting trees, reducing the use of non-biodegradable items and even lowering the volume of music systems to check sound pollution.A set of dos and don'ts were proposed by the Kokrajhar district administration for nearly 200 Durga Puja committees in the town as part of efforts to popularise the concept of “carbon-neutral” celebrations.“We proposed the idea as part of our efforts to have environmentally responsible festivities while preserving the religious and cultural essence of the festival.

It is very nice to see that nearly 50 per cent of the committees have responded very positively by significantly reducing the use of plastic items, planting trees and even controlling the volume of music systems,” Kokrajhar District Commissioner Pankaj Chakravarty told DH over the phone on Sunday.

Kokrajhar is situated about 200 km west of Guwahati.Durga Puja celebrations began on Friday and will continue till Wednesday, following which the Durga idols will be immersed in rivers.With a population of nearly 35,000 (2011 Census), Kokrajhar Municipal town has diverse communities, including Bodos, Bengalis, Assamese, Rabhas, Nepalis, Adivasis, Saranias and others, each peacefully celebrating their own festivals.Lotus theme, red-and-white decor to mark Durga Puja in BengaluruCarbon-neutral celebrationsUnder the concept of “carbon-neutral” celebrations, the district administration proposed several measures, such as encouraging the use of locally available and reusable materials, including bamboo, jute, recycled paper and other environmentally responsible alternatives, for pandals and decorations; promoting idols made from natural clay and other biodegradable materials, with non-toxic colours, to minimise environmental pollution, particularly during immersion; tree plantation; the use of solar energy and LED lights; responsible sound management; and encouraging waste segregation, responsible disposal and recycling, among other measures.“This is an encouraging beginning.
The drive is resulting in public awareness, with the concept being shared by many on social media platforms.
why_it_matters_bullets: Shifts federal policy priorities and legislative momentum ahead of upcoming electoral and administrative deadlines.

stories.primary_headline: Tensions flare again in Paris as France counts cost of worst unrest in years

primary_source.headline: Tensions flare again in Paris as France counts cost of worst unrest in years - Reuters
primary_source.content: Tensions flare again in Paris as France counts cost of worst unrest in years  Reuters

sources.headline: Tensions flare again in Paris as France counts cost of worst unrest in years - Reuters
France wakes up to one of its worst bouts of unrest in years; one dead, 500 cops injured
France counts cost of worst unrest in years - ThePrint

brief_bullets: Paris: France woke on Sunday to the wreckage of one of its most violent days of unrest in years after protests over high prices and public services left one demonstrator dead, hundreds of police injured and nearly 1,800 people arrested.Nationwide demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris, where police made a record 855 arrests.

Across France, police detained some 1,800 people and more than 500 officers were injured, the interior minister said.More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services.While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers."No room for violence in our Republic," President Emmanuel Macron posted on X as the unrest unfolded late on Saturday. "Those who have ransacked, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."Aucune place pour la violence dans notre République.Ceux qui ont cassé, attaqué les préfectures comme les commerces, pillé jusqu’à nos mairies, seront poursuivis et punis.Aux forces de l’ordre, garantes du droit à manifester, je dis le soutien de la Nation.Nous ferons tous…— Emmanuel Macron (@EmmanuelMacron) October 17, 2026 A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect.Unrest mars day of violent protest in France, as student movement turns nationalIn Paris, smashed shop windows, burnt-out bicycles and spray-painted slogans bore witness to a day that began largely with peaceful demonstrations but descended into violence.In Limoges, workers assessed the damage to the 143-year-old city hall, which was partially destroyed in an arson attack.The unrest has increased pressure on Macron and his government.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals, with a presidential election due next year.Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement.Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted in his city, while Marseille Mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial aid to support those businesses impacted by the violence.The protests began last month over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living.
France counts cost of worst unrest in years ThePrint.
why_it_matters_bullets: Shifts federal policy priorities and legislative momentum ahead of upcoming electoral and administrative deadlines.

stories.primary_headline: Tilak Varma relishes new role as finisher

primary_source.headline: Tilak Varma relishes new role as finisher
primary_source.content: Bengaluru: India’s T20I vice-captain Tilak Varma has never shied away from talking his heart out. And for someone who loves pace on the ball and batting at No. 3, dropping down to No. 5 or even No. 6 is not an ideal situation to be in.However, for Tilak, who rarely gets to bat in his preferred position in a changed set-up, versatility has been his biggest strength.&nbsp;Asian Games 2026 | Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma do the star turn as India beat Pakistan by 19 runs to defend titleFrom the third T20I against South Africa in Dharamsala in December 2025 to the T20 World Cup (Super Eights vs South Africa) in Ahmedabad in February, Tilak regularly batted at No. 3 for seven straight games.And since his debut, if not on some rare occasion, Tilak has been a standard in India’s T20 top-four. Once Sanju Samson returned to the XI to accompany Abhishek Sharma at the top, and with Ishan Kishan playing one drop, Tilak was pushed down the order as a floating option. He admits that the situation is “unfortunate”, but India’s vice-captain also understands what it means to be a team-player, while enjoying the role of a finisher. “It is not easy to change the numbers (batting) from No. 3 to No. 5 and No. 6. It will be slightly challenging. But I have been working on that, especially how to finish the games. I have said I love finishing the games for India,” Tilak said after the series-deciding fifth T20I was called off due to persistent rain.For me as an individual, if you see, it will be easier batting at 3. But unfortunately, I should bat at 5 or 6 because we have got that combination at the top right now. Kishan (Ishan) is batting at 3, and he is doing brilliantly. I think there is no option but to bat at five or six and do the job."Talking about his role clarity and preparation in his transition to a T20I finisher, Tilak highlighted he’s got all the shots in the book and is confident of changing positions with just a few sessions in the nets. And the numbers are impressive: averaging 65.66 in nine games.“We should do that (working on his skills as a finisher), otherwise, it will be tough. When you go in to bat as a finisher, if the ball comes in your arc, you should try to hit it for a six. Because, if you see in T20s, most of the time in this role, you get to bat a maximum of five or six overs.“If you see, I have been in this role in my childhood as well. I have got shots all over the ground. So I am confident that whether I bat at three or five, I have got the technique to adapt, and if I practice for a day or two, I can do any role for the team. Now even if I come back to No. 3, I can adapt within a day or two of practice. I am confident of batting anywhere,” he said.

stories.primary_headline: Delhi: Class 12 student stabbed to death outside school, five apprehended

primary_source.headline: Delhi: Class 12 student stabbed to death outside school, five apprehended
primary_source.content: New Delhi: A 17-year-old Class 12 student was allegedly stabbed to death outside a government school in southwest Delhi's Mohan Garden area following an altercation between two students over the prescribed school shoes, police said on Sunday.Five accused, including three minors and two adults, have been apprehended in connection with the murder, three of whom are students of the same school, they said.The incident took place on October 14 when a PCR call regarding a stabbing incident near a government school in Mohan Garden was received at 6.10 pm at the local police station. The victim, a resident of Mohan Garden, had sustained stab injuries and was taken to Tarak Hospital, where he succumbed during treatment, the police said.Class 11 student fatally stabbed in south Delhi; two heldAccording to an eyewitness, a Class 12 student of the same school, the dispute began after another student complained to a teacher that he was not wearing the prescribed school-pattern shoes. This led to a heated argument between the two, during which the latter allegedly threatened him.After school hours, when the student left the premises with his friends, including the victim, the other student allegedly instigated the remaining accused, following which the group assaulted them. During the attack, one of the assailants allegedly stabbed the victim, causing fatal injuries, the police said.The knife allegedly used in the crime was recovered near the school gate.The victim's father is an ex-serviceman and is currently employed as a gunman in Gurugram, police said.

stories.primary_headline: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial

primary_source.headline: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial
primary_source.content: In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemicsIs there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases.It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future. stories.primary_headline: They came to see Kolkata's famous pandals, but never returned home

primary_source.headline: They came to see Kolkata's famous pandals, but never returned home
primary_source.content: Kolkata: Pranjal Sarkar had no visible injuries anywhere else on his body. The only mark was that of a shoe on the left side of his face, a grim imprint of the brutal force of the footstep of an unknown person who may have unwittingly crushed the 13-year-old to death when the crowd surged at the Durga Puja pandal in Chorbagan in north-central Kolkata.Pranjal watched videos of the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotsab Samiti’s pandal on social media. The 13-year-old might not have fully grasped the “Beyond Sound” theme conceived and brought to life by artist Susanta Shibani Paul, but the sight of Goddess Durga and her four children, Kartik, Ganesh, Lakshmi and Saraswati, seated on a crescent moon amid dim, celestial lighting, caught his imagination. He insisted that the pandal be a must-see when his parents, Anukul Sarkar and Priyanka Sarkar, brought him from Agarpara in the North 24 Parganas district to Kolkata on the second day of the autumn festival.Little did Pranjal or his parents know that a danger lurked beneath the pandal’s surreal ambience, one that would turn the family’s Durga Puja outing into an unimaginable tragedy.The boy was one of the 19 people killed in the stampede at the pandal on Saturday. His parents survived, though. “He would have left for a tour to Shillong today with my sister and brother-in-law. Instead, I had to see the lifeless body of my nephew,” Pranjal’s maternal uncle said in front of the mortuary of Kolkata Medical College and Hospital on Sunday. “My brother-in-law could save seven or eight other children, but not his own son.”Even as the autumn festival unfolded across West Bengal, the stampede cast a pall of gloom over the families of the deceased and their neighbourhoods, from Kolkata and the Hooghly, Purba Bardhaman, North 24 Parganas and Nadia districts of West Bengal to Muzaffarpur in Bihar, turning what should have been a time of celebration into one of mourning.Kolkata stampede: Families mourn loss of loved ones as evening of festivity turned into heartacheSriparna Poddar, a 27-year-old nurse at a hospital in Kolkata, was often the first person her neighbours in Baidyabati, Hooghly, approached for healthcare advice. But on Sunday, she lay dead among the other victims of the stampede, while her family and neighbours waited to take home her mortal remains.Sandeep Bej, another 13-year-old boy, wanted to stay in his village in Madhabdihi in Purba Bardhaman for the Durga Puja celebrations but, at the last moment, went to Kolkata with his mother, Tagar Bej, 37, to see some of the city's pandals. However, the mother-son duo died in the stampede. So did Tagar’s sister, Piyali. Sandeep’s sister, Agamani Bej, was injured. “They were expected to return to their village on Sunday. But now only their mortal remains will return.”Ram Biswas came from Chakdaha in Nadia with his wife, Arati Sarkar Biswas, for pandal-hopping in Kolkata. He survived the stampede at Chorbagan but could not save his wife. Recalling the horror, Ram said that the crowd surged into the pandal after the ropes restricting entry were removed when it started raining. “It was dark inside, and people rushing in knocked others to the ground. Arati and I fell. I somehow got up and tried to pull her to her feet, but I couldn’t. My wife died before my eyes. I could do nothing,” Ram said on Sunday.For Abhishek Srivastava and his 13-year-old son, Ayansh, the trip to Kolkata was meant to be their first experience of the city’s famed Durga Puja celebrations. The two travelled from Muzaffarpur in Bihar to visit relatives in Agarpara, West Bengal, and went pandal-hopping with family members on Saturday. But both died in the stampede.Tania Biswas and Barnali Haldar, both 17, had planned their Maha Saptami outing well in advance. The Class XI students from Gouranga Nagar in New Town were close friends who had decided to wear sarees for the occasion. They set out with five other friends to visit the city’s Durga Puja pandals, but the outing ended in tragedy in Chorbagan, where both died in the stampede.Barnali’s father, Binod Haldar, who ekes out a living by pulling a rickshaw around New Town, learnt of his daughter’s death while he was still working. Her friends called him, and he rushed to the hospital, only to find that his elder child had already died. He spent the night outside the hospital mortuary. “My world has ended,” he said in a trembling voice, with tears rolling down his cheeks. “There will never be a Durga Puja in our lives again.”
